reasoning.Student A:
My goal is to maximize my chances of getting my most preferred school. The key insight is that the order I rank the schools only matters in selecting from my "obtainable set," and doesn't change which schools are in that set.

School y is my top choice and I have priority 1 there. This means y is almost certainly in my obtainable set.

School x is my second choice and I have priority 2 there.

School z is my third choice and I have priority 2 there.

School w is my least favorite and I have priority 1 there.

Since y is my top choice and I have top priority at y, I should rank y first. This guarantees that if y is obtainable (which is highly likely), I will be matched to y.

Next, I prefer x to z, so I should rank x higher than z. The relative ordering of x, z, and w will only matter if I am not matched to y.

Finally, I prefer z to w, so I should rank z higher than w.

Therefore, my ranking should be y > x > z > w.
